raw_response:
I am sixty years old and have farmed this land in Quzhou for forty years. I never went to school, but I know these fields better than any book. With 16.9 mu and four mouths to feed, I cannot afford to gamble. I stick to what works, watch what my neighbors do, and borrow a little from my son if a good input costs too much up front.

My backbone is the wheat-maize rotation on 10 mu. In early October I will rotary-till and sow improved wheat seed — about 30 jin per mu, the same amount I have used for years. I will put down roughly one and a half bags of compound fertilizer per mu at planting and topdress once in spring. That is about 32 kg of nitrogen, 20 kg of phosphorus, and 8 kg of potassium per mu if you weigh it, but I just call it a big bag and a small bag. I irrigate three times from my well: after sowing, at jointing, and at grain-filling. Water costs money to pump, but without it the wheat turns yellow and the yield drops. I spray pesticide three times — herbicide once and insecticide twice — when I see the bugs moving. If the spring rains do not fail, I expect about 1,000 kg per mu.

After harvest in early June there is barely a week before the maize must go in. I do not till — there is no time, and the no-till seeder works fine after forty years of doing it this way. I plant hybrid maize seed, one package per mu, and spread compound fertilizer at planting, about 100 kg per mu. That gives roughly 25 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate twice and spray twice for insects. I should get about 1,100 kg per mu.

The remaining 6.9 mu I split between cotton and chili. I put 4 mu into cotton because it is familiar — my mother grew it, and I know the rhythm. I rotary-till in spring, sow improved cottonseed in late April, and fertilize well: about 28 kg nitrogen, 12 kg phosphorus, and 10 kg potassium per mu, half at planting and half at flowering. I irrigate three times and spray about ten times for bollworms and aphids. I hope for 600 kg of seed cotton per mu.

Chili brings the best price, but it is the hardest on my back. On 2.9 mu I rotary-till, transplant in spring, and give it plenty of food — about 35 kg nitrogen, 18 kg phosphorus, and 18 kg potassium per mu — and water five times. I spray eight times to keep the rot and worms off. If the weather cooperates, I can get 3,000 kg per mu. I do not grow more because at my age I cannot bend that long, and my daughter-in-law already has enough to do.

I thought about cutting fertilizer to save cash, but two years ago my cousin did that and lost 200 kg per mu on his wheat. I would rather sleep with a little debt than risk an empty table.
